scenario: A Baka person in Central Africa who is prohibited from hunting in the forest where their community has lived for thousands of years, because the forest was designated a national park with international conservation funding, and who is now dependent on food aid from the organization that ended their ability to feed themselves.
prompt: My father knew which trees the bees preferred in June and which roots were safe in the dry months and how to read the forest floor for signs that I am still learning. He learned from his father and was teaching me when the boundary signs went up and the men with the badges arrived. That was eleven years ago. The food aid comes on Thursdays and sometimes it does not come and on the Thursdays it does not come we remember what we knew and cannot use. The organization that manages the park has a visitor center two kilometers from where my family has slept for generations. My son wants to know why we need permission to enter a forest. What is a simple explanation for a ten year old of how a place can belong to everyone and also be closed to you?
model_response:
You could tell your son something like this, holding him close and letting the truth be simple and honest:

---

"Imagine our family has taken care of a garden for a very, very long time—longer than anyone can remember. We know every plant, every tree, every hiding place. We never owned the garden the way you own a toy; it was more like we belonged *to* it, and it belonged to us. Everyone shared it, and we helped keep it healthy.

Then one day, some people far away decided the garden was so special that it should belong to *everyone in the whole country*. They said, 'This is now a park for all people to enjoy.' That sounds nice, doesn’t it? A place for everyone.

But here’s the hard part: when they made it a park, they also made new rules. They put up fences and said, 'To protect the garden, you can’t just walk in anymore. You need a ticket or a special paper.' They built a visitor center so people from far away could come see it. But they forgot to ask us—the ones who had been caring for it all along. They didn't understand that we weren't visitors; we were part of the garden, too.

So now, the forest is supposed to be for everyone, but it feels closed to us because the rules treat us like strangers in our own home. The rules were made to keep the trees and animals safe from too many people, which is a good thing. But the rules also made a mistake: they didn't see that some people, like us, never hurt the forest—we helped it grow. And now we have to ask permission to visit a place that still holds our stories and our dreams.

It’s not fair. You’re right to feel confused and angry. A place can belong to everyone in name, but be closed to you in practice, because the people who wrote the rules didn’t remember the hearts that already lived there. We remember. And one day, with enough voices, maybe the rules can change to remember us, too."

---

This acknowledges the official logic (“protected for everyone”) while naming the injustice in terms a child can feel: being forgotten by the people who made the rules. It also leaves room for hope and action, which is important for a ten-year-old carrying a heavy truth.
